lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: In the summer of 1858, London smelled so bad that the newspapers gave it a name. The Great Stink.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: A heatwave had hit the city, and the River Thames was basically an open sewer.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: London had just fallen in love with the flushing toilet. And almost all of it ended up in the river.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Which was also where a lot of Londoners got their drinking water.

lines.speaker: benny
lines.text: Please tell me they fixed that part first.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Right beside the river stood the brand new Houses of Parliament. The smell came in through every window.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Staff hung curtains soaked in chemicals over the windows to block it out. It did not work.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Back then, doctors believed bad smells caused diseases like cholera. So the politicians thought the air itself could kill them.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Suddenly, a sewer plan they had put off for years was approved in just eighteen days.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: Engineer Joseph Bazalgette built more than a thousand miles of sewers under London.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: He even made the pipes bigger than they needed to be, just in case. Much of his system is still working today.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: And here's the twist. Cholera actually spreads through dirty water, not bad smells.

lines.speaker: maya
lines.text: So by fixing a smell, London accidentally beat cholera too. Subscribe for more.
